summary:
On the outskirts of Havana, a cactus clings to existence. *Leptocereus wrightii*, endemic to Cuba, is now known from just ten surviving plants — a single remnant population occupying a fragment of land no larger than four square kilometers. Its only other known community vanished when the Villa Panamerica neighborhood was built, erased by the spread of the city.

What remains faces fire, grazing animals, and the continued pressure of urban growth. No new plants are regenerating. Without intervention, this quietly ancient species — part of a lineage stretching back millions of years — may disappear before it even carries a common name. Ten plants. One location. A world balanced on the edge.
